tips.title: A pairs with T, C pairs with G
tips.body: The **complementary base pairs** are **A–T** and **C–G**, joined by **weak hydrogen bonds**. Given one strand you can always write the other. Say **weak hydrogen bonds** — the word *weak* is in the specification and is worth a mark.

tips.title: Three bases, one amino acid
tips.body: A **triplet** of bases — a **codon** in mRNA — codes for **one amino acid**. So 30 bases code for $30 \div 3 = $ **10** amino acids. Divide by three, every time.

tips.title: Transcription copies, translation builds
tips.body: **Transcription** makes an **mRNA copy** of the gene, in the nucleus. **Translation** turns that message into a **chain of amino acids**, at the ribosome. Copy first, build second — the names say which is which.

tips.title: Genome and gene are not the same
tips.body: The **genome** is the **entire DNA of an organism**. A **gene** is **a section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein**. One is everything; the other is one instruction within it.

tips.title: Coding changes activity, non-coding changes quantity
tips.body: A variant in **coding** DNA alters the **amino acid sequence**, and so the **activity** of the protein. A variant in **non-coding** DNA affects **RNA polymerase binding**, and so the **quantity** produced. Activity against quantity.

why.matters:
A gene does one thing: it says what order to join amino acids in. Everything else an organism is follows from the proteins that come out of that — enzymes, keratin, haemoglobin, the receptors in a membrane.

So the code has to be copied accurately and read reliably, and both of those are in the structure. Complementary base pairs make the copying nearly automatic; a triplet code makes the reading unambiguous. The chemistry is the reason the information survives at all.

examples.title: Why the bonds holding DNA together are weak on purpose
examples.body:
The two strands are held by **hydrogen bonds** between complementary bases, and the specification insists on the word **weak**. That looks like a flaw in something that has to last a lifetime.

It is the point. The strands have to come apart — to be copied before a cell divides, and to be read whenever a protein is needed — and something that came apart only with difficulty would be no use. The strength is in the **number** of bonds, not in any one of them: millions of weak links hold, and a few at a time can be opened.

visual.alt: A table of the complementary base pairs: A with T and C with G, each pair joined by weak hydrogen bonds so the two strands can be separated for copying and for reading

examples.title: Why three bases and not two
examples.body:
There are four bases and about twenty amino acids to specify. Pairs of bases would give only 4 × 4 = **16** combinations, which is not enough. Triplets give 4 × 4 × 4 = **64**, which is more than enough.

So the code is read in threes, and the arithmetic follows: a coding sequence of **300** bases specifies **100** amino acids. That single division is most of the calculation in this topic, and it is also why adding or deleting one base is so damaging — everything after it is read in the wrong groups of three.

props.caption: Combinations available, against about 20 amino acids to name

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion: sixty-four combinations available from reading bases in threes against sixteen from reading them in pairs, where about twenty amino acids have to be named

examples.title: Why some mutations do nothing and some change everything
examples.body:
Most of the genome does not code for protein, so a variant there changes no amino acid at all. It can still matter — non-coding DNA affects **how much** of a protein is made and when — but the protein itself is unchanged.

A variant in **coding** DNA is different: it can alter the amino acid sequence, and if that changes the shape of an enzyme's active site the protein stops working. Same kind of change, two completely different consequences, and which one you get depends only on **where** it happened.

steps.title: The structure of DNA
steps.body:
**DNA is a polymer**, and the specification describes it in three parts.

**Two strands coiled to form a double helix.** The familiar twisted-ladder shape.

**The strands are linked by a series of complementary base pairs, joined together by weak hydrogen bonds.** Note **weak** — it is in the specification, and it matters: weak bonds can be separated to read or copy the DNA without breaking the strands themselves.

**DNA is made of nucleotides**, and each nucleotide consists of **a sugar and phosphate group with one of the four different bases attached to the sugar**.

**The four bases are A, T, C and G**, and they pair in a fixed way:

- **A pairs with T**
- **C pairs with G**

**This is what "complementary" means.** Because the pairing is fixed, **one strand determines the other completely**. Given `ATGCCTAGG` on one strand, the other must read `TACGGATCC`.

**Why that matters** is worth seeing now, because it explains two things at once. It is how DNA can be **copied** accurately — separate the strands and each acts as a template for a new partner. And it is how a gene can be **read** into mRNA, which is the first stage of making a protein.

**Extracting DNA from fruit.** The specification asks you to explain how this is done. The fruit is **mashed** to break up the tissue, then mixed with **detergent**, which breaks open the cell and nuclear **membranes**, and **salt**, which makes the DNA clump together. The mixture is **filtered**, and cold **alcohol** is added: DNA is insoluble in alcohol, so it comes out of solution as white strands that can be seen.

steps.title: Genome, gene and protein
steps.body:
**Two definitions the specification gives directly:**

**The genome is the entire DNA of an organism.**

**A gene is a section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein.**

One is the whole library; the other is a single instruction within it.

**How a gene codes for a protein.** *The order of bases in a section of DNA decides the order of amino acids in the protein.* Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and it is the **sequence** of bases that determines the **sequence** of amino acids.

**Three bases code for one amino acid.** A group of three is a **triplet** — called a **codon** when it appears in mRNA. So a gene of 30 bases codes for $30 \div 3 = $ **10** amino acids.

**And then the protein folds.** *These fold to produce specifically shaped proteins such as enzymes.* This is the step students most often omit, and it is where the whole point lies.

**Why the shape matters.** An enzyme works because its **active site** has a shape that fits its substrate. That shape is produced by the chain **folding**, and how it folds is determined by the **order of amino acids** — which is determined by the **order of bases**.

**So the chain of consequence runs:** order of **bases** → order of **amino acids** → the way the protein **folds** → the **shape** of the protein → what it can **do**. Being able to state that chain is what a top answer looks like, and it explains why a single change in the DNA can stop a protein working.

steps.title: How variants change the phenotype
steps.body:
**A genetic variant is a change in the DNA**, and where it occurs determines what it does. The specification treats two cases, and the distinction between them is examined.

**A variant in the coding DNA of a gene** affects the phenotype by **altering the sequence of amino acids**, and therefore **the activity of the protein produced**.

Follow the chain. A different base means a different **codon**. A different codon may mean a different **amino acid**. A different amino acid changes how the chain **folds**, so the protein has a different **shape** — and if it is an enzyme, its **active site** may no longer fit its substrate. The protein may work **less well**, or not at all.

**So a coding variant changes what the protein can do — its activity.**

**A variant in the non-coding DNA of a gene** affects the phenotype by **influencing the binding of RNA polymerase**, and therefore **altering the quantity of protein produced**.

Recall that **RNA polymerase binds to non-coding DNA located in front of a gene**. If that region changes, the enzyme may bind **more easily** or **less easily**. The protein itself is unchanged — it is made correctly — but **more or less of it** is produced.

**So a non-coding variant changes how much protein there is — its quantity.**

**The contrast in one line: coding affects activity, non-coding affects quantity.** Both can change the phenotype, and a question asking for the difference is asking for exactly this.

**Not every variant has an effect.** Most genetic mutations have **no effect** on the phenotype, some have a **small** effect, and **rarely** a single mutation will **significantly** affect it.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Say "weak hydrogen bonds".** The specification includes the word **weak**, and it is there for a reason: the bonds must be breakable so the strands can separate to be read or copied, without the strands themselves coming apart.

**Describe a nucleotide fully.** A **sugar** and **phosphate** group with **one of the four different bases attached to the sugar**. "A sugar, a phosphate and a base" is most of it, but attaching the base **to the sugar** is the detail that completes it.

**Take the chain all the way to shape.** Order of **bases** → order of **amino acids** → how the chain **folds** → the protein's **shape** → its **function**. Most answers stop at the amino acid sequence. The specification explicitly says the amino acids **fold to produce specifically shaped proteins such as enzymes** — the folding is the point.

**Get stage one right.** **RNA polymerase binds to non-coding DNA located in front of a gene** — not to the gene itself. That detail is what makes the non-coding variant question answerable later.

**Keep the two variants apart in one line.** **Coding → amino acid sequence → activity.** **Non-coding → polymerase binding → quantity.** Activity against quantity. This is the cleanest way to hold the distinction, and it is asked for directly.

**Do not overstate the effect of mutations.** **Most** have **no effect**, **some** a **small** effect, and **rarely** a single mutation **significantly** affects the phenotype. An answer implying every mutation causes disease has the balance wrong.

**Divide by three, and check it goes exactly.** A gene of 30 bases codes for 10 amino acids. If the division leaves a remainder, re-read the question — you have probably been given the number of amino acids rather than bases.

**Explain the fruit DNA extraction by what each step is for**: mash to break up the **tissue**, detergent to break the **membranes**, salt to make the DNA **clump**, filter to remove debris, cold alcohol to make the DNA come **out of solution**. Naming a step without its purpose scores less.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **DNA is a polymer**: **two strands coiled to form a double helix**.
- The strands are linked by **complementary base pairs** joined by **weak hydrogen bonds**.
- A **nucleotide** is **a sugar and phosphate group with one of four bases attached to the sugar**.
- The pairings are **A–T** and **C–G**, so one strand determines the other.
- The **genome** is the **entire DNA of an organism**.
- A **gene** is **a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein**.
- **Three bases (a triplet, or codon in mRNA) code for one amino acid.**
- The **order of bases** decides the **order of amino acids**, which decides how the protein **folds**.
- Folding gives the protein its **shape**, and the shape determines what it can **do**.
- **Transcription**: RNA polymerase binds to **non-coding DNA in front of a gene** and makes a **complementary mRNA** strand.
- **Translation**: the mRNA attaches to a **ribosome**, **codons** specify amino acids, **tRNA** brings them, and they **link to form polypeptides**.
- A **coding** variant alters the **amino acid sequence** and so the protein's **activity**.
- A **non-coding** variant alters **RNA polymerase binding** and so the **quantity** of protein.
- **Most mutations have no effect**; rarely one significantly affects the phenotype.
- **DNA from fruit**: mash, detergent, salt, filter, cold alcohol.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of DNA and explain how the order of bases in a gene determines the protein that is produced.
questions.solution:
**DNA is a polymer** consisting of **two strands coiled to form a double helix**. The two strands are linked by a series of **complementary base pairs**, which are joined together by **weak hydrogen bonds**.

The repeating unit is a **nucleotide**, and each nucleotide consists of **a sugar and a phosphate group, with one of the four different bases attached to the sugar**.

The four bases pair in a fixed way: **A pairs with T**, and **C pairs with G**. This is what *complementary* means, and it has an important consequence — **one strand completely determines the other**. Given `ATGCCTAGG` on one strand, the other must read `TACGGATCC`.

It is worth noting why the bonds between the pairs are **weak**. The strands need to be **separated** so a gene can be read, and DNA needs to be copied — but the strands themselves must stay intact. Weak hydrogen bonds between the pairs can be broken and reformed easily, while stronger bonds along each strand hold it together.

**A gene is a section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein**, and the **genome** is the **entire DNA of an organism**.

**How the base order determines the protein.** The **order of bases** in a section of DNA decides the **order of amino acids** in the protein. The code works in **triplets**: three bases — called a **codon** when read in mRNA — code for **one amino acid**. So a gene of 30 bases codes for $30 \div 3 = 10$ amino acids.

But the sequence of amino acids is not the end of the story, and this is the step most answers omit. The amino acids, once linked into a chain, **fold to produce specifically shaped proteins such as enzymes**.

**The folding is determined by the order of the amino acids**, because different amino acids attract and repel one another differently, so a given sequence folds into a particular three-dimensional shape.

**And the shape determines the function.** An enzyme works because its **active site** has a shape that fits its **substrate** — only a correctly shaped active site will do. Other proteins depend on their shape just as much, whether as structural fibres or as receptors.

So the full chain of consequence is: **order of bases → order of amino acids → how the chain folds → the shape of the protein → what the protein can do**. That chain also explains why a single change in the DNA can stop a protein working altogether: change one base, and you may change one amino acid, which may change the folding, which may leave an enzyme whose active site no longer fits.

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of protein synthesis, and explain how genetic variants in coding and non-coding DNA affect the phenotype differently.
questions.solution:
Protein synthesis happens in two phases: **transcription**, which makes a copy of the gene, and **translation**, which uses that copy to build the protein.

**Transcription.** First, **RNA polymerase binds to non-coding DNA located in front of a gene**. It is important that this is the **non-coding** region ahead of the gene, not the gene itself.

The enzyme then **produces a complementary mRNA strand from the coding DNA of the gene**. Because the bases pair in a fixed way, the mRNA carries an accurate copy of the gene's message. This happens in the **nucleus**, and the mRNA then leaves it.

**Translation.** The **mRNA attaches to the ribosome**. The message is read in groups of three: **triplets of bases (codons) in the mRNA code for specific amino acids**.

**tRNA transfers amino acids to the ribosome**, bringing the correct amino acid for each codon in turn. Finally, the **amino acids link to form polypeptides** — a chain which then folds into the protein's specific shape.

**How variants affect the phenotype differently** follows directly from those stages, and the two cases are cleanly distinguished.

**A variant in the coding DNA of a gene** affects the phenotype by **altering the sequence of amino acids**, and therefore the **activity of the protein produced**.

The reasoning is: a changed base gives a changed **codon**; a changed codon may specify a **different amino acid**; a different amino acid changes how the chain **folds**; different folding gives a different **shape**. If the protein is an **enzyme**, its **active site** may no longer fit its substrate, so the enzyme works less well or not at all. The **amount** of protein is unaffected — the cell makes just as much, but what it makes behaves differently.

**A variant in the non-coding DNA of a gene** affects the phenotype by **influencing the binding of RNA polymerase**, and therefore **altering the quantity of protein produced**.

Here the reasoning runs through transcription's first stage. RNA polymerase binds to the **non-coding region in front of the gene**, so a change there may make binding **easier** or **harder**. If it binds more readily, transcription happens more often and **more** protein is made; if less readily, **less** is made. The protein itself is **completely normal** — the coding DNA is unchanged — there is simply more or less of it.

**So the contrast is activity against quantity.** A coding variant changes **what the protein does**; a non-coding variant changes **how much of it there is**. Both can alter the phenotype, which is why non-coding DNA is not the "junk" it was once assumed to be.

Finally, it is worth keeping the scale of this in proportion: **most genetic mutations have no effect on the phenotype**, **some** have a **small** effect, and only **rarely** does a single mutation significantly affect it.

Protein synthesis happens in two phases: **transcription**, which makes a copy of the gene, and **translation**, which uses that copy to build the protein.

**Transcription.** First, **RNA polymerase binds to non-coding DNA located in front of a gene**. It is important that this is the **non-coding** region ahead of the gene, not the gene itself.

The enzyme then **produces a complementary mRNA strand from the coding DNA of the gene**. Because the bases pair in a fixed way, the mRNA carries an accurate copy of the gene's message. This happens in the **nucleus**, and the mRNA then leaves it.

**Translation.** The **mRNA attaches to the ribosome**. The message is read in groups of three: **triplets of bases (codons) in the mRNA code for specific amino acids**.

**tRNA transfers amino acids to the ribosome**, bringing the correct amino acid for each codon in turn. Finally, the **amino acids link to form polypeptides** — a chain which then folds into the protein's specific shape.

**How variants affect the phenotype differently** follows directly from those stages, and the two cases are cleanly distinguished.

**A variant in the coding DNA of a gene** affects the phenotype by **altering the sequence of amino acids**, and therefore the **activity of the protein produced**.

The reasoning is: a changed base gives a changed **codon**; a changed codon may specify a **different amino acid**; a different amino acid changes how the chain **folds**; different folding gives a different **shape**. If the protein is an **enzyme**, its **active site** may no longer fit its substrate, so the enzyme works less well or not at all. The **amount** of protein is unaffected — the cell makes just as much, but what it makes behaves differently.

**A variant in the non-coding DNA of a gene** affects the phenotype by **influencing the binding of RNA polymerase**, and therefore **altering the quantity of protein produced**.

Here the reasoning runs through transcription's first stage. RNA polymerase binds to the **non-coding region in front of the gene**, so a change there may make binding **easier** or **harder**. If it binds more readily, transcription happens more often and **more** protein is made; if less readily, **less** is made. The protein itself is **completely normal** — the coding DNA is unchanged — there is simply more or less of it.

**So the contrast is activity against quantity.** A coding variant changes **what the protein does**; a non-coding variant changes **how much of it there is**. Both can alter the phenotype, which is why non-coding DNA is not the "junk" it was once assumed to be.

Finally, it is worth keeping the scale of this in proportion: **most genetic mutations have no effect on the phenotype**, **some** have a **small** effect, and only **rarely** does a single mutation significantly affect it.

examTechnique.body:
Say **weak hydrogen bonds**, and describe a nucleotide as a **sugar and phosphate with a base attached to the sugar**. Take the gene-to-protein chain **all the way to shape and function**, not just to the amino acid order.

Remember RNA polymerase binds to **non-coding DNA in front of the gene**, and hold the contrast: **coding → activity**, **non-coding → quantity**.
examinerErrors: Omitting the word "weak" from hydrogen bonds.
Stopping the gene-to-protein chain at the amino acid sequence.
Saying RNA polymerase binds to the gene itself.
Saying a non-coding variant changes the protein's shape.
Using genome and gene as if they meant the same thing.
Implying that all mutations are harmful.
Listing the DNA extraction steps without their purposes.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer says **weak** hydrogen bonds and can explain **why** that matters — the strands must separate without breaking. It carries the gene-to-protein chain **all the way**: base order → amino acid order → **folding** → **shape** → **function**, and uses an enzyme's **active site** to make the point concrete. It knows RNA polymerase binds to **non-coding DNA in front of the gene**, which is what makes the non-coding variant explanation possible. It holds the two variant types apart in a single line — **coding alters activity, non-coding alters quantity** — and keeps mutations in proportion, noting that **most have no effect at all**.
